Today’s project: a cheerful “Things I Love” page with a title, three favorite things, colors you choose, and a surprise button. By the end, it will have its own link.

Seven small steps

Read, do, check the box. Nothing here can make your computer explode. Promise.

Meet the three helpers

You don’t need to memorize these. Just know who does what.

Codex / Claude CodeYour coding partner. You describe the result; it writes and edits the files.
GitThe project’s memory. Each “commit” is a named save point.
GitHubThe online home for your repository—the folder containing your project and its history.
Good to know: a repository (people say “repo”) is just a project folder with superpowers.

Choose your coding partner

Pick either path. They can both build the same project.

  1. Open the Codex app and sign in.
  2. Create a folder named my-first-website somewhere easy to find.
  3. Choose that folder as your project in Codex, then start a new chat.
  1. Install Claude Code and sign in.
  2. Create a folder named my-first-website and open Terminal in that folder.
  3. Type claude, press Enter, and follow the sign-in steps.

Ask for your website

Copy this prompt into Codex or Claude Code. Change the words in brackets if you want—or use it exactly as written.

Build a simple, cheerful website called “Things I Love.” Use plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript so it can be published with GitHub Pages. Include: - a big welcome heading - three cards for my favorite things: [sunny mornings], [good music], and [little adventures] - bright [purple, pink, and yellow] colors - a button that reveals a sweet surprise message Make it work well on phones and computers. Create index.html, styles.css, and script.js. Explain what you made in beginner-friendly language, then check that the page works.

You should see three new files:

index.html
styles.css
script.js
Why three files? HTML holds the words, CSS makes them pretty, and JavaScript makes the button do something.

Look, click, and tweak

Ask your coding partner to show you the page. Click the surprise button and resize the window. Then make it feel like yours.

Please preview my website for me. Check that the surprise button works and that the page looks good on a phone-sized screen. If you find a problem, fix it and explain the fix simply.

Want a change? Talk normally: “Make the title pink,” “Add my favorite movie,” or “The button feels too serious—make it playful.” Small requests are excellent requests.

Give the project a memory

Now turn the folder into a Git repository and make the first commit. The easiest way is to ask your coding partner:

Turn this project into a Git repository with the default branch named main. Add the website files and create the first commit with the message “Create my first website.” Do not publish anything yet. Tell me when it is done.
A commit is a save point, not a final decision. You can make as many as you like as the website changes.

Put the repository on GitHub

  1. Create a free account at GitHub, or sign in.
  2. Choose New repository. Name it my-first-website.
  3. Choose Public. Leave README, .gitignore, and license unchecked, then create it.
  4. Copy the repository URL from GitHub. It ends in .git.

Replace the example URL below with the one you copied, then give the whole prompt to your coding partner.

Connect this local repository to my empty GitHub repository at https://github.com/MY-USERNAME/my-first-website.git and push the main branch. If GitHub asks me to sign in or approve access, pause and tell me exactly what to click.
Privacy pause: never put passwords, API keys, addresses, or private notes in a public repository.

Publish with GitHub Pages

  1. Open your repository on GitHub and choose Settings.
  2. In the left sidebar, choose Pages.
  3. Under “Build and deployment,” set Source to Deploy from a branch.
  4. Select branch main, folder /(root), then choose Save.
  5. Wait a few minutes, refresh the Pages settings, and open your new link.

Your link will look like https://your-name.github.io/my-first-website/.

You made a real website.

Not a pretend exercise. Not “almost coding.” A real project with files, history, a GitHub home, and a public link. I’m very proud of you. ♥
